title: 5.3.34 Procedural vs OOP Writeup
description: Comparison of procedural and object-oriented programming.

aiGrader.prompt:
Write a comparison of procedural and object-oriented programming. Address all four sections below.

Question 1 — Definitions in your own words: What does procedural programming mean? What does object-oriented programming (OOP) mean? Do not copy definitions from the internet — use your own words.

Question 2 — A specific Q1 procedural example: Name a specific assignment or program you wrote in Q1 that used a procedural approach. Describe it in 1–2 sentences. Be specific — name the assignment.

Question 3 — A specific shplay OOP example: Name a specific place in your shplay code (A12.1 Collectible class, or an earlier class you wrote) where you used OOP. Describe how the class organized your code — what data and behavior did it group together?

Question 4 — When OOP wins: Describe one scenario (hypothetical is OK) where OOP is clearly the better choice over procedural code. Explain WHY in terms of at least one of the following: readability, extensibility, or separation of data and behavior.

rubric.title: Q1: Both terms defined in own words
rubric.description: Student defines procedural programming (code as a sequence of instructions, top-to-bottom or function-based flow) AND OOP (organizing code into classes/objects that bundle data and behavior) clearly and in their own words. Full credit requires both definitions to be accurate and personal. Half credit if one is clear and one is vague. Zero if definitions are missing or appear copied.

rubric.title: Q2: Specific Q1 procedural example named
rubric.description: Student names a specific Q1 assignment (by name or description) and provides a 1–2 sentence description of how it used a procedural approach. Full credit requires a specific reference — not a generic statement like 'I used procedural code in Q1.' Half credit for a vague but plausible reference. Zero for no example.

rubric.title: Q3: Specific shplay OOP example named
rubric.description: Student names a specific class from their shplay code (e.g., Collectible, Player, Enemy) and describes how that class organized their code — what properties and methods it contained, or how it reduced repetition. Full credit requires naming the class and explaining the organizational benefit. Half credit for a generic reference to using a class. Zero for no specific example.

rubric.title: Q4: OOP-wins scenario with reasoning
rubric.description: Student describes a specific scenario (real or hypothetical) where OOP is clearly the better approach and explains WHY using at least one of: readability (code is easier to understand), extensibility (easy to add more objects/types), or separation of data and behavior (object owns its own state). Full credit for a specific scenario plus 2–3 clear reasons. Partial credit for a specific scenario with only one reason or vague reasoning. Below expectations for a generic or missing response.

rubric.title: Writing clarity
rubric.description: Response is clearly organized and easy to follow. Deduct this point only for significant issues: incoherent structure, or writing that makes it difficult to assess the content. Do not deduct for length.
